newsitem.title: USA: Heredity trumps experience, even late in life-study.
newsitem.headline: Heredity trumps experience, even late in life-study.

text.p: A new study of ageing twins suggests that heredity trumps experience when it comes to cognitive skills late in life, researchers reported in Friday's edition of the journal Science.
The finding goes against the popular assumption that while genetics may play a key role in cognition among the young, experience supplants it as an influence as people age, the researchers said.

The scientists studied pairs of identical and fraternal twins over 80 years of age; identical twins share all the same genes, while fraternal twins share only half the same genes. The twins were found in Sweden, where a national registry lists 96 percent of all twins.
Even in their ninth decade, 62 percent of the twins' cognitive abilities could be attributed to genetic influences, roughly the same percent as for adolescents.

"What this study shows is that individual differences in cognitive abilities, such as spatial ability or memory, are due to genetic differences to a substantial extent, even very late in life," Robert Plomin, one of the article's authors, said in answer to a series of e-mail queries by Reuters.
What remains to be determined, Plomin said, is why some people in their 80s function well and others sink into decline.

Asked whether the study has any implications for treatment of problems in cognition of old age such as Alzheimer's disease, Plomin replied: "There is some evidence that that people who were high-functioning earlier in life may be less at risk for Alzheimer's.
"However, the best we can say now is the worn phrase that more research is needed," said Plomin, a professor at the Institute of Psychiatry, London.
Also unknown is whether people can do anything in their youth to increase cognitive function in their old age.
"The best thing you can do to increase your chances of good cognitive functioning in your older years is to have parents with good cognitive functioning late in life!" Plomin said.
